The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

derivations.claim: If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. Since $J:H\to\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism, the functional $J(e,-)$ is primitive, so Bezout's identity gives $f\in H$ with $J(e,f)=1$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$.

Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$.

For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$.

For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$.

The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$.

Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives $$ T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B, $$ because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry.
Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim.

Put representatives of $K,J$ and their chosen surfaces in separated balls, and join the surfaces by the connected-sum band away from the old basis curves. Their old first-homology bases together form a basis of the boundary-connected sum: collapsing the connecting band gives the wedge of the two surfaces, so first homology is their direct sum. Thus the matrix is $V_K\oplus V_J$, and [F2] gives $a(K\#J)=a(K)+a(J)$. The unknot has its disk surface with empty matrix and hence $a(U)=0$. By step 1.1 these calculations are independent of the separated representatives and chosen surfaces.

The inverse of $[J]$ is represented by $J^\dagger$, and therefore $J\#J^\dagger$ is concordant to $U$. Step 2.1 gives $a(J^\dagger)=-a(J)$. If $K$ and $J$ are smoothly concordant, their group difference $K\#J^\dagger$ is concordant to $U$, so $0=a(K\#J^\dagger)=a(K)-a(J)$. The smooth homomorphism is onto. Each positive generator $[V]$ of $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the image of the realizing knot from [F3]. The image of a group homomorphism is a subgroup, so it also contains the negative of every such generator. Every element of the presented integral group is a finite sum of signed generators, hence is in the image. This proves the entire smooth surjective-homomorphism assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

Every element of the integral algebraic concordance group has an invertible integral Seifert-matrix representative, allowing the empty matrix for the zero-rank representative. If $V$ is any such representative, the rule
$$
[V]\longmapsto[(\mathbb Q^{\operatorname{rank}V},V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)]
$$
defines an injective homomorphism into the rational isometric Witt group. An integral Seifert form represents zero in the integral group if and only if it is itself metabolic. These are finite algebraic assertions and require no choice principle; knot-derived forms retain their separately stated choice assumptions.

For a monic irreducible polynomial $p\in\mathbb Q[t]$ with $p(0)\ne0$, put $p^*(t)=p(0)^{-1}t^{\deg p}p(t^{-1})$. For each such self-reciprocal polynomial $p=p^*$ other than $t-1$, let $G_p$ be the subgroup of the rational isometric Witt group generated by structures whose characteristic polynomial is a power of $p$. Then restriction to the generalized primary subspaces induces an isomorphism
$$
G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{p=p^*,\ p\ne t-1}G_p.
$$
A pair of distinct reciprocal primary factors contributes a metabolic structure and therefore contributes zero. Only finitely many components of any given class are nonzero. No choice principle is needed.

Let $p\in\mathbb Q[t]$ be monic, irreducible, and self-reciprocal, with $p(0)
e0$ and $p
e t-1$. Put $E=\mathbb Q[t]/(p)$, write $\alpha=t+(p)$, and give $E$ the involution $\iota(\alpha)=\alpha^{-1}$. If $p
e t+1$, the primary component $G_p$ of the rational isometric Witt group is isomorphic to the hermitian Witt group of $E$ with this involution. Here the latter group is generated by finite-dimensional nonsingular hermitian forms, with orthogonal direct sum as addition and forms having an isotropic half-dimensional $E$-subspace set to zero. If $p=t+1$, the same conclusion holds with the group generated by even-dimensional nonsingular symmetric forms over $\mathbb Q$, modulo metabolic forms. For a semisimple primary isometry, the comparison sends a hermitian form $h$ to $(\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb Q}h,\alpha)$ on its underlying rational vector space. These comparisons require no choice principle.

Let $E/F$ be a quadratic extension of number fields with its nontrivial involution. In the hermitian Witt group $W(E/F)$, the kernel of all signatures is killed by $4$. The joint signature image is a free abelian subgroup of $\mathbb Z^s$ of rank at most $s$, where $s$ is the number of real places of $F$ at which $E$ becomes complex. No choice principle is required.

Let $W(\mathbb Q)$ denote the Witt group of nonsingular symmetric bilinear forms over $\mathbb Q$, with orthogonal sum as addition and metabolic forms set to zero. For every such form $q$, four times its Witt class equals its signature times the class of the four-dimensional identity form. In particular, the kernel of the signature is killed by $4$, including its restriction to the subgroup of even-dimensional classes. The signature image is $\mathbb Z$ on the full group and $2\mathbb Z$ on the even-dimensional subgroup.

In the integral algebraic concordance group put
$$
F_b=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_n=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-n^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q_q=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-(3q-1)/4\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $b,n$ range over positive integers and $q$ ranges over primes congruent to $3$ modulo $4$ other than $3$. The classes $[F_b]$ are independent of infinite order, each $[P_n]$ has exact order two, and each $[Q_q]$ has exact order four. The three families together generate their direct sum, isomorphic to
$$
\mathbb Z^{(\mathbb N)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{(\mathbb N)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^{(\mathbb N)}.
$$
Moreover the classes $[P_n]$ have linearly independent images in $G_{\mathbb Z}/2G_{\mathbb Z}$. These are pure algebraic assertions about the displayed forms; no choice principle is required.

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a countable abelian group and $s:G\to\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z$ a homomorphism whose kernel $K$ satisfies $4K=0$. Then $K$ is precisely the torsion subgroup of $G$, and for cardinals $r,u,v\le\aleph_0$,
$$G\cong\mathbb Z^{(r)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{(u)}\oplus(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^{(v)}.$$
If $G$ contains elements $f_i,p_i,q_i$, indexed by positive integers, such that the $f_i$ are integer-linearly independent, the order-two elements $p_i$ have linearly independent images in $G/2G$, and the $2q_i$ are linearly independent order-two elements with $4q_i=0$, then $r=u=v=\aleph_0$.

A rational structure is specified, after one finite basis choice, by its dimension and two finite rational matrices; the isometry and nonsingularity conditions select a subset of this countable set. An integral Seifert lattice is likewise specified by a finite integer matrix. The corresponding presented groups are quotients of the countable sets of finite signed lists of these matrices: finite lists of rationals or integers have explicit natural-number codes, so a countable union over their lengths is countable. Quotients are countable by the surjection from these codes. This argument does not identify the two types of object. Use the injection [F2] to regard $G_{\mathbb Z}$ as a subgroup of $G_{\mathbb Q}$ for the rest of the proof.

For each primary group of [F3] other than $t+1$, the involution on $E$ is nontrivial. Indeed if its distinguished generator equalled its inverse, its irreducible polynomial would divide $t^2-1$; $t-1$ is excluded by invertibility of $I-T$ and $t+1$ was separated. If $F=E^{\sigma}$, choose $0\ne\delta$ with $\sigma\delta=-\delta$. Every $z\in E$ has the unique decomposition $(z+\sigma z)/2+\delta(z-\sigma z)/(2\delta)$ with coefficients in $F$, so $E/F$ is quadratic. Take all hermitian signatures at real places of $F$ where $E$ becomes complex, and take the ordinary rational signature on the $t+1$ component. These form a homomorphism $s:G_{\mathbb Q}\to\bigoplus_{j\in J}\mathbb Z$. The index set $J$ is at most countable: there are countably many rational irreducible polynomials and finitely many real places for each number field. Each individual class has only finitely many primary components, so its total signature has finite support. With [A1] fix an enumeration of this index set, adding zero coordinates if needed, to put the target inside $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z$.

If $s(x)=0$, each of the finitely many nonzero primary components of $x$ has all its signatures zero. By [F4] four times each such component is zero; the primary direct-sum isomorphism [F3] gives $4x=0$. Thus $4\ker s=0$. The same holds for the kernel of $s\iota$ on $G_{\mathbb Z}$, since $\iota$ is injective. Applying [F6] separately to these two countable groups gives decompositions of each with at most countable free, order-two and order-four multiplicities. In particular every torsion class has order dividing four; the proof has used signatures to identify all torsion, rather than merely exhibiting some finite-order classes.

In either group, the elements $F_b,P_n,Q_q$ of [F5] meet the three infinitude tests of [F6]. A finite nonzero integer combination of the $F_b$ cannot be torsion: if some nonzero multiple vanished, projection to each distinct primary factor would contradict the infinite order of its $F_b$. The $2Q_q$ are independent order-two elements, by distinct primary factors and exact order four. For the rational quotient by doubles, project to the quadratic primary factor of $P_n$, identified with a hermitian Witt group by [F3], and then take hermitian rank modulo two. This is a homomorphism because metabolic hermitian forms have even rank. The two-dimensional rational structure of $P_n$ has rank one over its quadratic field, so the homomorphism takes value one there; it vanishes on the other $P_m$ by their distinct primary factors, and on every double by its target $\mathbb Z/2$. Hence the $P_n$ are independent modulo doubles in $G_{\mathbb Q}$ as well as in $G_{\mathbb Z}$, the latter also following directly from [F5]. Thus the $P_n$ are independent in the quotient by doubles in each group. This last condition forces independent order-two summands after splitting; independent order-two elements alone would not suffice, since doubles of order-four elements also have order two. There are infinitely many indicated primes $q$ by the finite Euclidean argument in [F5].

By [F6] and step 4.1, all three multiplicities in both decompositions from step 3.1 are infinite, and their countable upper bounds make them precisely $\aleph_0$. This is the displayed abstract group isomorphism for each of $G_{\mathbb Q}$ and $G_{\mathbb Z}$. The integral result here follows from its proved injection, the shared exponent bound, the splitting argument and the actual integral families. No assertion that primary summands split integrally, no identification of the rational group with its integral subgroup, and no unspecified integral localization or coupling theorem is needed for this abstract isomorphism. In particular the allowed $t+1$ component of the original rational Definition has been retained throughout.

A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

Assume full AC for the knot Seifert-pairing convention. Let $V\in M_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be an invertible Seifert matrix and put $B=V+V^T$ and $T=V^{-1}V^T$ on $\mathbb Q^{2g}$. Then $B$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T$ is an invertible $B$-isometry, and $I-T$ is invertible; hence $(\mathbb Q^{2g},B,T)$ is a rational Seifert isometric structure.

Let $H$ be a free abelian group of rank $2g$ and let $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ be a bilinear form. Write $H_{\mathbb Q}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and extend $V$ $\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to $H_{\mathbb Q}$. If $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of dimension $g$ and $V(x,y)=0$ for all $x,y\in L$, then $M=H\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand of $H$ and $V|_{M\times M}=0$.

derivations.claim: From [F1], $V-V^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $1$, so this is a positive-rank integral Seifert lattice satisfying the false claim's hypothesis.

By [F3], the associated rational form is $B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}$. For every nonzero $(m,n)\in\mathbb Q^2$, $B((m,n),(m,n))= -2(m^2+mn+n^2)=-2(m+n/2)^2-3n^2/2<0$, so there is no rational isotropic line to which [F4] applies. In particular, for every nonzero integral vector the Seifert self-pairing $-(m^2+mn+n^2)$ is negative; [F2] rules out a rank-one metabolizer. This lattice refutes the claim.
